items.extracted_excerpt: OpenAI is raising Security Bug Bounty rewards and introducing report quality, loyalty, and priority campaign bonuses for independent security researchers.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: We’re raising rewards in OpenAI’s Security Bug Bounty program to further encourage independent researchers to pursue vulnerabilities in OpenAI software that our testing may have missed. We’re also introducing new incentives for researchers to earn more for higher quality vulnerability reports. Independent security researchers play an essential role in protecting technology across the industry. At OpenAI, incentivizing responsible disclosure is a core part of our security model, complementing our Defense Factory work, where our engineers use our models to find weaknesses, reproduce them, and test fixes. Today’s updates are designed to encourage and empower researchers, and to continue building a collaborative, community-first security environment. We’re more than quadrupling the midpoint of our reward ranges for medium, high, and critical findings on average. A critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000. Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses. The full details are available in our security bug bounty program(opens in a new window). High-quality reports will be eligible to earn a bonus multiplier on the base bounty. A reliable proof of concept that isolates the bug, shows when it can be exploited, and demonstrates its impact gives us a head start on a fix. The quality multiplier recognizes the extra work that makes a finding especially useful. To build long-term relationships and continuously empower our security community, we are introducing a tiered loyalty bonus program. This 5-tier system provides scaling bonuses to recognize, support, and celebrate researchers who consistently partner with us in making AI technology safer for everyone. To support community engagement as technology evolves, priority campaigns will feature dedicated bonus pools for newly launched features. These short-term campaigns give researchers early, high-reward opportunities to test new developments and be recognized for their early contributions. All scenarios and historical awards are illustrative. If you’ve already submitted a report and we haven’t yet awarded a bounty, we’ll apply the new reward ranges. For bounties we awarded in the 30 days before this announcement, we’ll pay you the difference if your finding would have earned more under the new ranges (Base Award + Loyalty Awards). On November 20–21, our security team will be at PROMPT2PWN(opens in a new window) in Oakland, where researchers can test targets in person. If you’ll be there, we’d love to hear what you’ve been working on and how to partner with you. Thank you to everyone who has taken the time to investigate a lead and report it to us. We want OpenAI to be a team you come back to when you find something we’ve missed.

items.extracted_text_for_analysis: We’re planning our next internal security sprint at OpenAI, bringing new researchers and security partners together with our own teams to use our models to test and strengthen our systems. We’re partnering with Cathedral, whose researchers will use OpenAI’s models alongside our teams to challenge our defenses, bringing differentiated expertise and approaches to finding weaknesses and helping us protect our platforms. We’re also making improvements to our Security Bug Bounty program including more than quadrupling our rewards for critical findings. We want researchers to challenge our assumptions and help strengthen both our systems and the methods we use to defend them. This is part of our ongoing effort to use AI to continuously find and fix weaknesses in our systems. Our last sprint showed what this approach can deliver. We dedicated 25% of our product engineers to finding and fixing weaknesses in our systems. Using Codex, engineers investigated findings, reproduced vulnerabilities in isolated environments and prepared patches for review. We’re building on that work because traditional cyber defenses alone are no longer sufficient. Recent incidents across the industry show how quickly threats can emerge and how important it is to build continuous defensive loops to find and fix weaknesses before attackers do. Keeping the defender’s window open requires organizations to use frontier cyber capabilities to harden their systems. We’re using our most capable models to strengthen our own defenses and making them available to Daybreak customers. We’ve committed $1 billion in subsidized access over six months for frontline defenders protecting essential services and digital infrastructure. We’re also sharing our architecture and lessons from the last sprint, alongside our blueprint for empowering cyber defenders across industry and government. We’ll keep advancing our models, using them to strengthen our own systems, and expanding access for trusted defenders. Keeping the defender’s window open will take action across the industry, and that work needs to start now.

items.summary_en: How OpenAI built Pando, a Git-compatible backend designed for the scale of development that Codex makes possible.
items.extracted_excerpt: How OpenAI built Pando, a Git-compatible backend designed for the scale of development that Codex makes possible.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Over the past year, the size and demands on our monorepo have increased at a staggering pace. It was clear that we needed to revamp our source control system to scale to the level of concurrent work that Codex makes possible. We built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories, without interrupting any engineering work or changing how our team uses Git. Pando now powers all development in OpenAI’s monorepo. Pando is designed to meet two ambitious goals: first, horizontally scalable writes, optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches. And second, maximize read throughput, so clients can download data fast enough to fully saturate their available network bandwidth. We met these goals while retaining compatibility with the Git protocol and client, enabling both our engineers and agents to seamlessly adopt Pando into their existing workflows. In production, Pando cut median push latency by nearly 5x. It now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. Here, we’ll cover our motivations for building a new source-control system, along with why we chose to retain compatibility with Git. We’ll compare our system with common approaches to scaling Git, describing why Pando is uniquely capable of meeting OpenAI’s scalability needs. We also discuss what’s next, and how we’ll continue contributing to Git to support agent-scale work. Codex has changed the scale and pace of development at OpenAI, enabling engineers to do far more work in parallel. That means more branches and pushes, more merges, and more fetches and clones from development environments, research jobs, and CI. These demands compound. One engineer now has several changes ready for CI at once, and each push can set several jobs fetching the same commit. Starting around the end of last year, the systems supporting our monorepo were struggling to keep up. We suffered slow fetches and pushes along with failed merges, with reliability at times falling below 90%. Had we reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo? Git grew out of a community that exchanged patches to the kernel via email. For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed. When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work. We saw a way to keep that familiar workflow while rebuilding the backend to handle pushes to different branches in parallel and serve the same history to many readers concurrently. Building on Git as the foundation of our source-control workflow meant that improvements to the client could be useful beyond OpenAI. We wanted to contribute those improvements from our copy of Git(opens in a new window) to upstream, sharing them with the broader community. Scaling a source control system has two essential dimensions: many writers pushing to different branches, and many readers fetching the same history. Pando optimizes for both. First, Pando coordinates updates to each branch independently. Updates to unrelated branches can proceed in parallel, and a reader fetching a branch gets the history needed for that revision. The tradeoff is that a reader looking at several branches can see them at different points of time. Second, Pando reuses packfiles (Git’s format for compressing multiple objects together) across fetches instead of generating an individual packfile for each client. A client may download some objects it already has, but the server can serve the same bytes to many clients with little computation. These choices let us scale writes across branches and serve reads from caches. To see how they fit together, let’s start with how Git stores and transfers history. Git must be able to keep two parts of a repository in sync: objects and references. A Git repository records snapshots of files and the history connecting them as a graph of objects. An object may be either a blob, tree, commit, or tag. Blobs hold the content of an individual file, and trees associate names with blobs or other trees to form a directory structure. Commits point to a root tree and zero or more parent commits, forming the history of your repository. Objects are identified by a hash of their type and contents. Objects are also immutable: recording a changed file creates a new blob, while unchanged files and directories can reuse existing objects. Branches and tags are references, or “refs”, that point to commits. Committing on a branch creates a new commit and updates the branch’s ref to point to it. Git stores objects in either a “loose” or “packed” state. Loose objects are stored in individual files identified by their object ID. Packed objects are stored together in a packfile, enabling similar objects to be stored as deltas against one another. In Git, an object is reachable from a commit if Git can find it by following links from that commit through its parents, trees, and blobs. During a fetch, the client tells the server which commits it wants and which it already has. The server finds the objects reachable from the wanted commits, excludes those it knows the client already has, and sends the remainder as a packfile in the same format Git uses on disk. A full clone starts without any objects, so it needs all the objects reachable from the history being cloned. A push transfers objects in the other direction by asking the server to update one or more refs. The client uses the server’s set of advertised refs to avoid sending objects the server already has. The pack being sent can therefore depend on existing objects: receiving the pack alone is not enough to reconstruct the new history. Replicating a Git repository means keeping both objects and references available across multiple servers. Before a replica can serve a reference’s new value, it must be able to supply the objects reachable from that value. The service also needs to coordinate competing reference updates, i.e., pushes that try to move the same branch from the same old tip to different new commits. Systems that impose a single order on all writes to a repository can make pushes to unrelated branches wait on one another. When any server receives a push, the incoming packfile is copied and sent to all replicas in parallel. To publish the push, a majority of replicas must accept the ref update. items.extracted_excerpt: OpenAI’s Grid Protectors Program will work with utilities to help future compute campuses support grid reliability and protect consumer electricity costs.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Today we’re launching the Grid Protectors Program, a national effort to support affordable, reliable electricity for families and businesses in the communities where we build. Working with utilities, regulators and policymakers, we’ll develop arrangements for our future campuses to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain. Whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. Our goal is to make campus flexibility a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most. With U.S. data center capacity projected to exceed 100 gigawatts by 2030(opens in a new window), we have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to strengthen the electric grid by building campuses that can adjust their power use when communities need it most. Through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how quickly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized. Depending on local needs and the equipment available, we will also work with grid operators to supply power from on-site generation or storage, and use batteries and power controls to smooth changes in demand. Power lines, substations and other grid infrastructure builds are a fixed cost whether demand is low or high. By using more electricity when the grid has room and reducing our use when it is under strain, we can help pay for that infrastructure while limiting the need for costly upgrades to meet peak demand. That can help keep costs down for other customers. America needs more electricity to support economic growth, and AI is becoming a significant part of that demand. Families and small businesses should not be asked to subsidize a compute campus’s electricity needs. We’ve always been committed to paying our own energy costs, including the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve our campuses. Large computing facilities should pay their costs and help utilities manage the systems they depend on. For our planned Effingham County campus, we have committed to pay the full infrastructure and electric-service costs required to serve the project. Once the campus is operating, we can reduce the power we draw during times of need, helping preserve electricity for other customers. Our agreement with Georgia Power also includes(opens in a new window) up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response, freeing up power to help keep air conditioning running in hundreds of thousands of homes during extreme heat. For scale, that is equivalent to the average electricity demand of roughly 700,000 households. That’s more households than Washington, D.C., and Boston combined. These compute facilities are much different than data centers built even a few years ago, allowing us to be flexible in our power demand. This means we can turn down our demand so that families, small businesses, and other ratepayers will continue to have power. Building grid assets is expensive and Georgia Power says this flexibility can reduce the amount of new generation it needs to build to serve future growth. Although the campus is still in development, we intend for Effingham to serve as a pilot for Grid Protectors, building on an agreement that already provides a model for future campuses. Imagine a restaurant in a vacation town. It needs enough tables and kitchen space for the busy season, but it has to pay for that capacity year-round. Regular customers help keep it in use and cover the bills when tourism slows. We are proposing to be that regular customer. Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times. Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest. We still need to pay the costs our campuses create; the goal is for other customers to benefit, too. Our agreement also contributes to Georgia Power’s broader plan to lower costs for customers. The utility projects approximately $950 million in annual customer savings beginning in 2029(opens in a new window) from its portfolio of large-load agreements and expected growth, including Project Camellia. It estimates a benefit of at least $15 a month for a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours. The Georgia agreement is a starting point. At OpenAI, through our Grid Protectors program, we see an opportunity to help communities keep the lights on even in times of emergency and high demand. We will work with utilities, regulators and policymakers to develop practical arrangements for the campuses we build in the future-arrangements that reflect local grid needs, help campuses support the grid when it is under pressure, and pay the costs we create. Long-term contracts and financial assurances can protect other customers if a project is delayed, reduced or canceled. Flexibility cannot replace investment in new energy supply and transmission. Alongside those investments, our Grid Protectors program can help make the grid more reliable and protect families and small businesses from bearing the costs of AI infrastructure. That is the standard we want our compute campuses to meet.

items.extracted_excerpt: Introducing LifeVal, a benchmark measuring how well AI helps people complete everyday tasks, from finding childcare to managing finances and government paperwork.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: OpenAI’s mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. For the more than one billion people who currently use ChatGPT every week, we want to build AI that can help with the practical challenges of everyday life, like finding childcare, accessing government services, creating a budget, preparing for school, modifying recipes, ordering groceries, designing workout plans, and more. When someone is looking for help making their life easier, they need more than advice or a chat response. To be a truly helpful personal assistant, ChatGPT should be able to take actions that actually get things done. To measure model performance over time on everyday tasks, we built an evaluation of tasks covering areas where users wanted the most help from AI and personal agents. We used this evaluation to track and drive improvement in model performance on everyday tasks over the past year. Background To identify the tasks people value most, we started with two large studies that track how people spend time in both the U.S. and internationally: the American Time Use Survey(opens in a new window) and the Multinational Time Use Study(opens in a new window). Together, these datasets provide a detailed catalog of everyday life tasks that people do across different demographics, times of day, and seasons. To understand where people would most value AI assistance, we expanded on these existing surveys with a new demographically representative survey of 3,995 respondents. For each task, we asked a variety of questions to identify the areas where everyday people most wanted help from a personal assistant. The resulting tasks span the most important areas that people want help with, including caregiving, health, education, household administration, personal finances, shopping, and accessing government services. Individual task examples Below are some examples of how our current models perform on practical workflows from everyday life. Our latest models score very highly on many LifeVal tasks. See more Over the past year, we’ve trained our models to become much faster, more capable, and more aligned on browser use, computer use, and connectors tasks. Enabling these capabilities in ChatGPT also expands the types of tasks the model can help with, helping move ChatGPT beyond a chat tool and towards a truly agentic personal assistant. Why this matters To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, we need to measure and improve model progress on what matters in the lives of everyday people. That means going beyond academic assessments of model knowledge and actually measuring how well AI models can help people navigate decisions, manage everyday responsibilities, and get meaningful things done. We are hopeful that LifeVal represents a step towards that goal.

items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Qodo builds context into AI code review with Codex Qodo brings organizational context and codebase standards into Codex, helping developers catch P0 issues across repositories. Qodo(opens in a new window) builds AI tools for code review and software quality, giving coding agents the organizational knowledge they need to understand the code they change. Co-founder and CEO Itamar Friedman calls it “the coding agent’s best friend.” Qodo uses OpenAI models including GPT‑6 Astra to gather engineering knowledge, review code, and monitor software quality. Its Codex plugin brings that context and review into developers’ coding sessions. “We love OpenAI models. We want the frontier, the best reasoning models, but also those that are really fast.” Itamar describes customer environments that can span 10,000 or more repositories, where a local code change can break a downstream service, even if it looks correct on its own. Qodo built a plugin in the Codex marketplace to address this. “Codex is really good at taking a local task and completing it in an efficient way,” Itamar says. Qodo’s plugin gives Codex access to codebase knowledge, organizational rules, and independent review through Qodo’s Agentic Toolbox. With context, Codex can account for dependencies across repositories, including those hosted by different Git providers or services connected through Kafka. “Qodo will make that connection and will help Codex look at the software as a whole and not miss those P0 bugs,” Itamar says. Before Codex starts writing code, it can use Qodo’s plugin to retrieve the relevant codebase rules and pull request history and patterns. After Codex makes the changes, Qodo reviews them and returns its findings directly to Codex in the same session, before the developer opens a pull request. Nnenna Ndukwe, Qodo’s AI Developer Relations Lead, sees developers using this workflow to build features and tackle technical debt with GPT‑6 models in Codex. They are automating the handoff between Codex’s coding work and Qodo’s independent review. “That’s what I’ve been seeing developers do, which is really exciting because GPT‑6 is extremely capable,” Nnenna says. Itamar describes coding and review agents as “yin and yang”: one creates code, the other challenges it. Each role needs its own setup and context and may involve multiple agents. His vision is for agents to discuss findings and “surface only what they don’t accept” for human review. Developers would become planners and reviewers, able to inspect unresolved issues alongside the agents’ discussion, context, and prior developer decisions. “That’s how you create trust,” Itamar says. “I think it makes the whole process overall more efficient,” Nnenna adds. “We get to leverage the best parts of our expertise.” Internally at Qodo, Nnenna has been using GPT‑6 Astra’s Extra High and Ultra effort settings in her own automated development workflows as well as knowledge work. “What does Codex not do? I love everything that Codex does. I love the idea of combining AI and automation.” Nnenna schedules Codex to report on what she accomplished during the week and where she could focus or improve next. She also uses it to research conversations about agentic engineering on social platforms and suggest ideas for developer content. When it comes to her own code changes, she schedules Codex to analyze her work and suggest agent skills to create or refine. Itamar sees an opportunity to use OpenAI’s recently launched Decisions API to choose which rules and agent skills apply at each stage of development, rather than rely on language models for every decision. He cites an example where the Decisions API could select which of 200 rules need checking before a language model reasons through the relevant ones, helping to make selection faster and cheaper while improving the quality of the review. “The Decisions API is an immense opportunity for us to bring more trust to the process,” Itamar says. Qodo’s approach combines “the best aspects of artificial intelligence and the best aspects of traditional software engineering and scripting,” Nnenna says. Company knowledge guides coding agents, independent review checks their work, and human expertise resolves the questions that remain. This creates the foundation of what Itamar describes as a software factory: a system customers could assemble and own, bringing coding and review agents together with an understanding of how software changes in production. With OpenAI, Qodo is building a future where coding agents put more of a company’s experience to work and developers can focus their judgment where it matters most.

items.extracted_text_for_analysis: 基調講演を行うSakana AI Chief Scientific Advisorのユルゲン・シュミットフーバー教授 （English Report Below.） 2026年10月26日、Sakana AIは東京・一橋講堂でシンポジウム「From World Models to Real-World AI — 日本から拓くAIの新時代」を開催しました。9月にChief Scientific Advisorとしてお迎えしたユルゲン・シュミットフーバー（Jürgen Schmidhuber）教授は、1980年代から、最初のTransformer（正規化なし線形Transformer）、深層ニューラルネットワークの事前学習と蒸留、現代的な世界モデル、生成的・敵対的なネットワークによる人工好奇心、再帰的自己改善など、いまの深層学習と生成AIの土台となる数多くのアイデアを切り拓いてきた研究者です。20世紀で最も引用されたAI論文となった1997年のLSTM論文の共著者でもあります。教授の基調講演と、2018年に教授と論文「World Models」を共著した共同創業者兼CEOのDavid Haとの対談に、日本各地から400名を超える方にご参加いただきました。 このシンポジウムで、Sakana AIは自社による事前学習モデルの開発に乗り出すことを明らかにしました。チーフサイエンティストの秋葉拓哉が、事前学習から自社で開発する言語モデルシリーズ「Sakana Sawara（仮称）」を発表しました。最初のモデルとなる小規模な「Sawara Small（仮称）」は、順調に進めば2027年春に公開する予定です。 このシンポジウムは、Schmidhuber教授を迎えたSakana AIの意気込みをお伝えし、日本の企業や研究機関の皆さんとともにAIの次の時代を切り開いていくスタート地点として企画しました。本記事では、各講演と対談の内容を、講演録の形でお伝えします（抜粋し、読みやすさのために一部の順序を入れ替えて編集しています）。 目次 司会を務めたSakana AI Chief of Staffの田附千絵子 オープニング：From World Models to Real-World AI：David Ha 最初に、共同創業者兼CEOのDavid Haが登壇しました。 Sakana AI CEOのDavid Ha 知能は制約から生まれる 今日着ているTシャツには、世界モデルの図がプリントされています。Schmidhuber教授が1990年に描いたものです。当時は計算のコストがいまより100万倍から10億倍も高く、論文の図も手で描いて貼り付けていました。いまではAIサイエンティストが一緒に論文を書く時代になりましたが、1980年代から90年代のイノベーションがいまにつながっていることを、ときどき思い出すのは良いことだと思います。 私がSNSでよく言っている持論に、「基盤モデルは、人類史上もっとも速く価値を失う金融資産の一つだ」というものがあります。AIのモデルをつくる会社を始めた私にとって、これは悩ましい問題です。日本は、この分野で世界とどう戦えばいいのか。 私の信念は、計算資源とデータを大量に投入してモデルを大きくし続けることだけが道ではない、というものです。知能は制約から生まれます。いまのAIは豊かさによってスケールしていますが、生物の知能は欠乏の中から生まれました。進化は、より少ない資源でより多くをなすものを選びます。脳も、言語も、文化も、制約が知能を生むことの証拠です。 10年ほど前、私はAIの研究にのめり込み、OpenAI Gymの難しい課題にいくつも挑戦していました。二足歩行ロボットの課題では、ニューラルネットワークだけでなく、ロボットの体の大きさや使うエネルギーも最小にするよう制約をかけてみました。すると、AIは虫のように歩く小さなロボットを生み出しました。では、制約をまったくなくすとどうなるか。AIが見つけたのは、脳を持たず、ゴールに向かってただ倒れ込む巨大なロボットでした。AIが脳を持つためには、制約が必要なのです。 Schmidhuber教授の論文との出会い ピクセルから車を運転するカーレースの課題では、エージェントに世界モデルを持たせました。未来に何が起きるかを予測し、世界を潜在空間で表現できるようにしたのです。 そのとき私がしたのは、Jürgenがいつも言うように、過去の研究をさかのぼることでした。そこで出会ったのが、世界を微分可能にする1990年の論文から、2015年の「On Learning to Think」に至る、教授の世界モデルの一連の論文です。アルゴリズム情報理論から人工好奇心まで、多くの概念がまとめられていて、とても刺激を受けました。エージェントをコントローラー（C）と世界モデル（M）に分けて考える、という発想もそこで学びました。 その後、Jürgenと共同で書いたのが、NeurIPSで発表した論文「World Models」です。この論文では、エージェントが世界モデルの見る「夢」の中で学習できることを示しました。こうした考え方は、いまでは自動運転やロボティクスなど、多くのイノベーションの土台になっています。 Sakana AIの研究と、日本のAI主権 2023年、私はLlion Jones、伊藤錬とともにSakana AIを創業しました。サカナは日本語で魚のことです。知能は一匹の魚ではなく、群れにある。私たちはそう考えて、集合知のアプローチをとっています。そして、資源の限られた日本の会社として、他社と同じことはしたくありません。群れとは少し違う方向に泳ぐ、赤い魚でありたいと考えています。 「知能は一匹の魚ではなく、群れにある」と話すDavid これまでに、脳に着想を得たContinuous Thought Machines、誤差逆伝播法を使わずに1,000層のネットワークを学習するPC-ALM、今年Nature誌に掲載されたAIサイエンティスト、そしてSchmidhuber教授のゲーデルマシンの考えをLLMで実装したダーウィン・ゲーデルマシンなどの研究を発表してきました。 では、日本は世界の競争の中でどうAIをつくっていくのか。私は、日本のAI主権を3本の柱で考えています。一から技術をつくれる「事前学習」、日本の価値観に合わせる「事後学習」、そして世界のフロンティアモデルと自社のモデルを組み合わせて性能を引き出す「オーケストレーション」です。オーケストレーションではSakana Fuguを、事後学習ではSakana Namazuを提供しています。 そして最後の柱が、事前学習です。私たちは、自社のモデルの事前学習に取り組み始めます。詳しくは、このあとチーフサイエンティストの秋葉拓哉が話します。 私たちが描いているのは、エージェント・ネイティブな言語モデルと世界モデルを事前学習し、互いに連携させて難しいタスクに取り組ませ、AIサイエンティストによる自己改善のループでモデルを磨いていく計画です。この計画は、Jürgenの論文にあるコントローラーと世界モデルの構成と、大きくは変わりません。いま手に入る技術を組み合わせれば、過去の優れたアイデアを生かして、フロンティアを押し広げることができるのです。 基調講演：Jürgen Schmidhuber 続いて、Jürgen Schmidhuber教授が基調講演を行いました。 ニューラルネットワークは230年前に生まれた Davidが1990年に私が描いた図のTシャツを着てきてくれたことを、とても誇りに思います。 現代のAIは、人工ニューラルネットワークに基づいています。脳には約1,000億個のニューロンがあり、それぞれが平均1万ほどの結合を持っています。結合の強さは最初はランダムですが、学習によって強くなったり弱くなったりします。そうして、車の運転や翻訳など、さまざまなことができるようになるのです。 では、人工ニューラルネットワークを発明したのは誰でしょうか。1940年ごろのアメリカの誰かだと思っている人もいますが、それはまったくの誤りです。発明されたのは230年前、1795年から1805年のことです。ガウスは1795年に、1990年代に「2層の線形ニューラルネットワーク」と呼ばれたものとまったく同じ仕組みを手にしていました。入力と出力をつなぐ重みを調整して、訓練データに対する二乗誤差を最小にする。当時は「最小二乗法」と呼ばれていました。最初に発表したのは、1805年のルジャンドルです。いま有名な企業が取り組んでいることの核心は、このGauss–Legendreのネットワークと同じです。主な違いは、いまのネットワークのほうが深いことです。 ちなみに、若きガウスが有名になったのは1801年、小惑星ケレスの位置を予測したときでした。観測の途中で太陽の陰に隠れたケレスが、次にどこに現れるか。ガウスはこの方法で「次のトークン」を予測し、見事に当てたのです。 日本で生まれた深層学習の源流 では、深層学習は誰がどこで発明したのか。1965年、当時のソビエト連邦のウクライナで、イヴァフネンコ（Ivakhnenko）とラパ（Lapa）が始めました。Ivakhnenkoの1971年の論文では、8層のネットワークで英国経済の時系列データから次の値を予測しています。 1967年には、日本の甘利俊一氏が、層ごとではなく全体を一度に学習する、エンドツーエンドの深層学習を示しました。計算がいまより何十億倍も高価だった時代に、5層のネットワークです。1970年にはフィンランドのリンナインマー（Linnainmaa）が、いまGoogleからSakana AIまで使っている誤差逆伝播法を発表しました。 日本からのもう一つの大きな貢献が、1979年の福島邦彦氏による最初の畳み込みニューラルネットワーク、ネオコグニトロンです。1986年には、これを手書き数字の認識に応用した有名な映像があります。1988年には、日本の研究室にいたウェイ・ジャン（Wei Zhang）氏が、福島氏の畳み込みネットワークを誤差逆伝播と組み合わせ、文字認識に応用しました。Zhang氏は1990年代に、これをさらにスケールさせています。今日のコンピュータービジョンの中核である畳み込みニューラルネットワークは、日本で発明され、さらに発展し、スケールしたものなのです。 せっかく日本に来たので、現代AIの発展においてこの国で起きた本質的な出来事を紹介したいと思いました。 ガウスから福島邦彦氏まで、現代AIの源流をたどるJürgen 1990年の世界モデルと人工好奇心 ニューラルネットワークへの私たち自身の貢献はもっと後、1990年のこの図から始まります。小さなロボットと、それを動かすコントロールネットワークがあります。入力の中には「R」と書かれたものがあります。報酬です。ロボットには痛みのセンサーがあり、自分の行動の評価を入力として受け取ります。 これは、いま「再帰的自己改善（RSI）」と呼ばれているものに欠かせない要素です。RSIとは、何かを学ぶだけでなく、学び方そのものを改善し、さらにその改善の仕方も改善していく、というように再帰的に学ぶシステムのことです。そのためには、環境からの評価の信号をネットワークに入力する必要があります。それが、この図にはすでにありました。 そこに、2つ目のネットワークを加えます。ロボットの行動と入力を見て、次に何が起きるかを予測するネットワーク、つまり世界のモデルです。良いモデルがあれば、計画を立てられます。頭の中で行動を試し、予測される報酬が多く、痛みの少ない行動を選べるのです。 しかし最初のうち、モデルは何も知りません。そこで、自ら実験を考え出す「人工科学者」が必要になります。赤ちゃんはWorld Wide Webをダウンロードして学ぶわけではありません。手を動かすと目に入る映像が変わる。その変化を予測しながら、物理を学び、リンゴが落ちることを学び、泣けば親がどう反応するかを学びます。自分の実験で、自分に必要なデータを選んで集めているのです。 私が1990年に発表した最も単純な方法では、世界モデルが誤差を最小化しようとする一方で、生成的なコントローラーは同じ誤差を最大化しようとします。モデルがまだ学べる余地のある場所を見つけると、コントローラーは報酬を得ます。世界について知らなかったことを教えてくれる実験を考え出したことへの、「エウレカ」の報酬です。多くの人がその変種を実装し、いまでは敵対的生成ネットワーク（GAN）と呼ばれていますが、私はこれを「人工好奇心」と呼んでいました。 1991年、「奇跡の年」 ただ当時は、深層学習がまだうまく動きませんでした。何千ステップも前の出来事が何千ステップ後に影響するような、長い時間差を扱えなかったのです。 そこで1991年、私たちはこの問題を解くための論文を立て続けに書きました。その成果は、いまのChatGPTの「P」と「T」につながっています。「次のものを予測する」という事前学習で長い系列を圧縮する手法。同じ論文で示した、あるネットワークの知識を別のネットワークに移す蒸留。そして、Transformerの最初の変種です。私は「Fast Weight Controller」と呼んでいましたが、いまでいう線形Transformerそのものです。2020年に「線形Transformer」と呼ばれるようになりました。線形なので、計算量はテキストの長さに比例してしか増えません。計算量が二次で増えるいまのTransformerは、テキストが1,000倍になると計算が100万倍必要になります。データセンターに巨額の投資が必要な理由の一つは、ここにあるのです。 同じ1991年、私の優秀な教え子のセップ・ホッフライター（Sepp Hochreiter）が、卒業論文で深層残差学習の原理を示しました。線形の活性化関数を持ち、自分自身への結合の重みが1.0の、とても単純なユニットを考えてみてください。誤差を時間をさかのぼって伝えても、つねに1.0を掛けるだけなので、何千ステップたっても何も変わりません。これが勾配降下法による非常に深い学習を可能にするもので、LSTMの核心です。これはのちに、2015年5月に私たちが「ハイウェイネットワーク」として発表した最初の深い残差フィードフォワードネットワーク、そしてその後の「ResNet」へとつながりました。 1991年当時、こうした研究に関心を持つ人はいませんでした。ある学会で発表したとき、聴衆は若い女性一人だけでした。「お嬢さん、気まずいけれど、今日はあなただけに話すことになりそうです」と言うと、彼女は「いいですよ。でも急いでください。次の発表者は私なんです」と答えました。それでも、コンピューターは5年ごとに10倍安くなり、いまでは当時より1,000万倍安くなりました。だからこそ、私たちが当時発表した技術は、いま皆さんのスマートフォンの中で動いているのです。 細部をシミュレーションしない計画 Davidがスライドで示したのは、より良い計画の方法です。素朴な計画は、世界モデルを使って未来をミリ秒単位でシミュレーションします。チェスや囲碁には十分ですが、本来やるべきことではありません。 ここからパリに行く計画を立てるとき、電話をつかむ手の動きまでシミュレーションする人はいません。タクシーを呼ぶ、空港に行く、チェックインする。いくつかの重要な点だけを押さえた、コンパクトな計画を立てます。 2015年に私が提案したのは、コントローラーが世界モデル（M）の隠れユニットに問い合わせを送るという方法です。Mは、YouTubeの動画をすべて見てきたかもしれないし、ロボットの経験を大量に持っているかもしれない。コントローラーは、学習するプロンプトエンジニアです。いま解きたい問題に関係のある内部表現だけに注意を向け、そこから答えを引き出して、自分の行動を変えていきます。その問い合わせは英語でも日本語でもなく、数値ベクトルの列です。単純な問題なら一から解いたほうが早いでしょう。しかし興味深い問題はどれも、巨大なモデルの奥に眠るアルゴリズム的な情報から大きな恩恵を受けるはずです。2018年には、蒸留を使ってコントローラーとモデルを一つにまとめる論文も書きました。もっとも、2018年のより有名な論文は、世界モデルが実際に役立つことを見事な実験で示したDavidの論文のほうです。 画面の外のAIへ ここで、少し広い歴史の文脈に目を向けましょう。今日お話ししたことの多くは、ドイツと日本で起きました。
